report:
## Conclusion: Partially Supported — With Important Caveats

The claim that eating dark chocolate lowers stroke risk is **supported by observational evidence** but **not yet confirmed by large randomized controlled trials**.

### What the Evidence Shows

Multiple meta-analyses of prospective cohort studies have found an inverse association between chocolate consumption and stroke risk. A meta-analysis of five prospective studies found a relative risk of 0.81 for high versus low chocolate consumption, and 0.86 for every additional 50 g/week of intake ([Frontiers in Nutrition, 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1696220/full)). A Swedish study found a 17% lower stroke risk among men consuming the highest amounts of chocolate ([American Academy of Neurology](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/1099)). A BMJ systematic review and meta-analysis also concluded chocolate consumption was associated with reduced cardiometabolic disorders, including stroke ([BMJ, 2011](https://www.bmj.com/content/343/bmj.d4488)).

### Important Caveats

1. **Most evidence is observational**, meaning it cannot prove causation. Chocolate consumers may differ in other lifestyle factors.
2. **Large randomized trials are inconclusive.** The COSMOS trial (500 mg/day cocoa flavanols) showed only a modest, non-significant benefit for cardiovascular events including stroke ([Springer, 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10654-026-01382-6)).
3. **Dark chocolate specifically** has been linked to reduced cardiovascular risk factors like blood pressure, but Mendelian randomization studies have not definitively established a causal link to CVD outcomes ([Nature Scientific Reports, 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-50351-6)).
4. Many commercial chocolate products are high in sugar and calories, which could offset benefits.

### Bottom Line

Dark chocolate (high cocoa content) is *associated* with lower stroke risk, likely through flavanol-mediated improvements in blood pressure and endothelial function. However, definitive causal proof from large randomized trials is lacking. Moderate consumption of high-cocoa dark chocolate may be a reasonable part of a heart-healthy diet, but it should not be relied upon as a primary stroke prevention strategy.
